Uncertainty modeling
In the problem discussed earlier, several parameters such as energy price, γ, renewable power47,48,49,50, PR, load demands, PC, QC, IC, EVs energy consumption, TCE, EVs charge rate and capacity, CR, \(\overline{S}_{EV}\) and \(\overline{I}_{EV}\) are uncertainty. To manage these uncertainties in resource scheduling, methodologies like robust, probabilistic, or stochastic programming are employed. Probabilistic and stochastic and approaches require examining numerous scenarios, which extend the convergence time and necessitate deriving a probability distribution function for each parameter as uncertainty4,18. This derivation often involves extensive statistical studies over long periods, such as a year, proving time-intensive4. Robust programming, on the other hand, offers a more streamlined approach by efficiently modeling these unknowns. It tackles the problem with significantly fewer assumptions than stochastic and probabilistic methods, providing expedient solutions without extensive scenario generation. Robust programming effectively accounts for the worst-case scenario tied to uncertainties, thereby yielding a solution that can withstand prediction errors in unknown parameters51. This approach mandates an uncertainty variable matrix. In this context, the uncertainty matrix \(\overline{u}\) as defined by (31) includes predicted value of uncertainties. Uncertainty variable matrix (u) is in Eq. (32). The structure of this matrix indicates that the number of rows corresponds to the number of buses (nb) in the system while number of columns (nc) are calculated based on nc = (6 + nh) × nt + 1. nh and nt shows number of harmonics and operation hours. Lastly, this framework outlines a set for the n-th row (Un) as Eq. (33)51. \(\tilde{u}\) is deviation of uncertainty, and UB is Uncertainty Budget that ranges between 0 and 1. A UB of zero aligns with a deterministic model whereas any other value indicates a robust approach. \(\left[ {\overline{u} - \tilde{u},\overline{u} + \tilde{u}} \right]\) is defined flexibility in handling uncertainty adjustments.
In this section, we explore the use of Adaptive Robust Optimization (ARO) to address uncertainties. ARO excels in extracting both the most resilient optimal solution and the worst-case scenario simultaneously. In this approach, for a problem defined as minx ∈Γ(x) f(x), the worst-case scenario is incorporated by adding maxu ∈ U to the problem. This results in the expression maxu ∈ U minx ∈Γ(x, u) f(x,u), aligning with the ARO objective to derive robust solution in worst-case scenario51. Here, x represents the primary variables such as power, voltage, and current in the proposed design. U encompasses uncertainty set as defined \(\bigcup\limits_{n} {U_{n} }\). Γ(x) denotes a set of constraints like Eqs. (2)-(28), while f(x) is the objective function (1). The inclusion of the variable u in f and Γ, maxu ∈ U minx ∈Γ(x, u) f(x,u) arises from their dependence on the uncertainty variable. To tackle this problem, we first derive dual model of minx ∈Γ(x) f(x), noted as max g(κ, ω), where κ and ω are dual variables pertaining to equality and inequality constraints in Γ(x). The details of dual formulation are expressed in51. The set Λ(κ, ω) outlines the dual constraints, and g(κ, ω) serves as the objective function of the dual problem. Details on obtaining Λ(κ, ω) and g(κ, ω) for minx ∈Γ(x) f(x) can be found in reference51. The problem then stabilizes as maxu ∈ U max g(κ, ω) or max g(κ, ω). Accordingly, the robust formulation include dual model of primal problem, (1)-(28), and uncertainty set constraint, u ∈ U. In this robust model, the objective function includes two continuous variables as products of dual and uncertainty variables. Given its convex nature, several solutions can be obtained efficiently through linear programming solvers like CPLEX52. Flowchart of the robust model shows in Fig. 2.
Numerical results
Case study
94-bus Portuguese distribution grid with a base power of 1 MVA and a nominal voltage of 15 kV as Fig. 353 is tested in this section. A comprehensive description of the network’s distribution substations and lines can be found in53. Peak load data is also sourced from53 for several buses, while hourly load values are derived by scaling the daily load factor curve based on the peak load values54,55,56,57,58. This load factor curve is depicted in Fig. 4, as noted in18. The energy procurement prices for the SDN are determined for three load periods: $16/MWh during low load (1:00–7:00), $24/MWh during medium load (8:00–16:00 and 23:00–24:00), and $30/MWh during high load (17:00–22:00), as outlined in4. It is advised to maintain the bus voltage range of the principal frequency component between 0.9 and 1.05 per unit59,60,61,62,63. The network includes nonlinear loads characterized by 6-pulse rectifier types installed at buses 7, 21, 49, 58, 65, 84, and 90. Additionally, it is important to note that the harmonic current of these loads (h ≠ 1) depends on the apparent power of the connected load (\(I_{C\,h} = \vartheta_{h} \sqrt {\left( {P_{C} } \right)^{2} + \left( {Q_{C} } \right)^{2} }\)). The loads in the system exhibit individual harmonics ranging from 5 to 43, with the harmonic coefficient ϑ for these harmonics being referenced in28. The permissible current flowing through the distribution substation at a harmonic frequency component for a voltage level of 15 kV is determined based on the IEEE 519 standard, detailed in37. According to this standard, the maximum allowable harmonic voltage is limited to 3%, or 0.03 per unit. In the specified network, seven FRIESs (F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, and F7) are implemented, with their locations indicated in Fig. 3. The peak active and reactive loads for these FRIESs are set at 0.2 MW and 0.1 MVAr respectively. As per22, the consumer participation rate in the DRP at each FRIES is 50%. FRIESs F1, F2, F6, and F7 are equipped with Wind Turbine (WT) and Photovoltaic (PV) systems, each rated at 0.3 MVA. The remaining FRIESs have renewable unit capacities of 0.5 MVA. For each harmonic (h ≠ 1), the power electronic converter capacity of RESs (\(\overline{I}_{R}\)) is set to 5% of their rated value (\(\overline{S}_{R}\))23. The hourly active power output of the RESs (PR) is calculated as the product of rated capacity (\(\overline{S}_{R}\)) and the daily power rate curve of RESs, as illustrated in Fig. 4 for WT and PV systems23. In FRIESs F3 to F5, EVs can charge with a maximum capacity of up to 200 EVs per station, while other FRIESs support up to 150 EVs. The number of EVs assigned to each time is determined by multiplying the total number of EVs with the EV penetration rate. The daily penetration rate curve for EVs is also depicted in Fig. 423,28. The efficiency of the chargers is rated at 92%, while additional technical details such as charging rate, charger capacity, and energy consumption per EV are provided in3,4,18,23,28. Within each harmonic frequency, the allocated capacity (\(\overline{I}_{EV}\)) remains at 5% of the rated value (\(\overline{S}_{EV}\))28. Furthermore, FRIESs do not include any nonlinear loads, which results in IC being zero. The combined pollution coefficients for emissions such as CO2, SO2, and NOx amount to 918.2 kg/MW5, while the minimum permissible value for the WSI is specified at 0.8 p.u.18. The proposed scheme is versatile and can be implemented across various distribution networks, resources, and active loads without constraints. Adjustments are required only for the problem’s scale by modifying the setting parameters within the linearization techniques. Essentially, as the problem’s size grows, the number of line segments also increases, resulting in the circular plane being approximated to a regular polygonal plane with a greater number of sides.
Results and discussion
This section focuses on implementing the proposed scheme using the General Algebraic Modeling System (GAMS) software framework, version 50.2.0 for year 2025. Following this, the linearized robust problem is addressed by leveraging the CPLEX solver52. In this approach, five linear segments are employed as part of the conventional piecewise linearization technique. Additionally, a circular plane is approximated to a 45-sided regular polygon format28. As referenced in51, the uncertainty deviation (\(\tilde{u}\)) is set to \(UL \times UB \times \overline{u}\), where UL indicates the uncertainty level.
A) Identifying the Optimal Solver for the Proposed Scheme: The Pareto front of the suggested design is depicted in Fig. 5 for the deterministic model with zero uncertainty level (UL = 0). This front is derived using five values for each weighting coefficient (0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1). For cost-related coefficients (ξC = 1, ξE = 1, ξT = 1, and ξV = 1), the minimum and maximum objective function values, namely Cost, EM (Environmental Metrics), TVH (Total Voltage Harmonics), and VSI (Voltage Stability Index), are computed. According to Fig. 5, the cost ranges from $835.1 to $2371.2, while EM varies between 22.3 tons and 36.7 tons. TVH spans from 219.7 p.u. to 407.5 p.u., and VSI fluctuates between 20.1 p.u. to 22.9 p.u. The changing range of each objective function on the Pareto front is calculated as the difference between these extremities: $1536.1 for Cost, 14.4 tons for EM, 187.8 p.u. for TVH, and 2.8 p.u. for VSI. Furthermore, Fig. 5 reveals that the directions of change for the objective functions are not uniform. For instance, an increase in VSI corresponds with a reduction in operational costs due to the role of low-cost, environmentally-friendly resources like FRIESs. These resources must inject high levels of active power into the grid to reduce energy costs, which in turn increases substation flow toward the upstream network compared to scenarios without FRIESs. This leads to higher power losses and over-voltage in substation lines, thereby escalating VSI values. FRIESs also depend on renewable units and EVs aggregations for harmonic control. To achieve cost reduction, high active power must be injected by these components, which can compromise their ability to manage reactive power and harmonic currents. Consequently, cost reductions often accompany an increase in TVH. Similar trade-offs are observed between EM and TVH. In Fig. 6, the compromise solution based on the Pareto front is presented using the fuzzy decision-making approach. Results from nonlinear programming (NLP) and linear programming (LP) models are juxtaposed here for the proposed scheme. NLP solvers such as IPOPT, CONOPT, and DISOPT are analyzed alongside LP solvers like CPLEX, CBC, and CONOPT52. Notably, NLP algorithms often yield varying results instead of a single optimal solution. Among these, IPOPT exhibits superior performance in terms of efficiency and convergence speed compared to CONOPT and DISOPT, achieving smaller values for Cost, EM, and TVH while maintaining higher VSI values. It also boasts reduced computational time (CT), making it faster in achieving convergence according to Fig. 6(a). However, Fig. 6(b) indicates that LP solvers generally deliver an optimal and unique solution with lower Cost, EM, and TVH values (and higher VSI values) than IPOPT while significantly reducing computational time compared to all NLP solvers. Among LP solvers, CPLEX stands out as particularly effective in non-convex nonlinear problems due to its better optimization outcomes and lower computational time compared to alternatives. Additionally, disparities in compromise points are evident across NLP algorithms due to differences in their optimal solutions. In contrast, LP solvers exhibit consistent compromise conditions. Comparing Figs. 5 and 6 demonstrates proximity between the compromise points and their respective minimum (or maximum) function values for all objectives. For instance, at the compromise point, the Cost function deviates by approximately 14.8% ((1067.2 – 835.1)/1536.1) from its minimum value, with 1536.1 representing its full range of fluctuation. Similarly, deviations for EM and TVH are calculated at 43.75% and 31.6%, respectively. For VSI, the deviation from its maximum point stands at 32.1%.
B) Robust model analysis: Robust optimization results is presented in Table 2, which outlines the objective functions, including Cost, EM, TVH, and VSI, at the compromise point in relation to uncertainty level (UL) for different uncertainty budgets (UB). The table demonstrates that when UL increases with UB set to 0, there is no change in the objective functions. This is because, in such cases, the deviation of uncertainty variables remains zero (i.e., UB = UL = 0), making the scenario identical to that of the deterministic model. Consequently, alterations in the uncertainty level do not impact the values of the objective functions. However, when UB is set to 0.5 (UB = 1), an increase in UL to 0.9 (0.5) leads to an increase (or decrease) in the values of Cost, EM, and TVH (or VSI). For instance, as shown in Table 2, a rise in UL causes increased load, PC, QC, IC, energy prices, γ, energy consumption of EVs, TCE, while reducing the production capacity of RESs (PR), EV charging rates (CR), and the capability of EV chargers to manage reactive power and harmonic currents (\(\overline{S}_{EV}\) and \(\overline{I}_{EV}\)) under the worst-case scenario when compared with the deterministic model. As a result, energy demand and prices rise while energy production declines in the worst-case scenario. Thus, an increase in UL ultimately elevates (or reduces) Cost, EM, and TVH (or VSI) in the robust model relative to the deterministic design. For cases where UL > 0.9 (UL > 0.5) at UB = 0.5 (UB = 1), the values of these objective functions reach saturation and remain constant at their levels corresponding to UL = 0.9 (UL = 0.5). This implies that with higher values for UL and UB, energy prices and demand experience the maximum rise, while energy production capacity sees the steepest reduction under worst-case conditions compared with the deterministic scenario. Consequently, solutions derived under these circumstances represent the most robust optimal point. This demonstrates that the proposed design for optimal power management of FRIESs in the network can endure up to a 45% maximum deviation due to uncertainties associated with load, RESs, EVs, and energy prices (calculated as UL × UB × 100 = 0.9 × 0.5 × 100). As highlighted in Sections "Uncertainty modeling" and23, the solution region under worst-case scenarios is more constrained than in the deterministic model. This inherently increases computational effort for the robust model. Table 2 reveals that higher UL and UB values significantly extend computation times compared to the deterministic model baseline where UL = UB = 0. From an economic perspective, the proposed plan introduces a cost model (Eq. 1) reflecting the expense of energy purchased by the distribution network from its upstream counterpart. The outcomes of this cost evaluation are depicted in Figs. 5 and 6 as well as Table 2. Table 2 specifically delineates costs for different robust models. The difference in cost between UL = 0 (deterministic model) and UL ≠ 0 (robust models) captures the expense incurred for retrofitting the distribution network against uncertainties associated with load variations, energy prices, renewable units, and EVs.
(C) Evaluating the economic and technical condition of SDN: To assess the impacts of the proposed approach on operational, security, environmental, economic, and power quality conditions, five distinct case studies were conducted as follows: Case I: SDN load flow analysis without FRIES, Case II/III/IV: Scheme incorporating only RESs/DRPs/EVs in FRIES, Case V: Implementation of the proposed design. The results for UB = 1 and UL = 0.45 are illustrated in Fig. 7. Based on this analysis, it is evident that RESs and DRPs significantly reduce energy losses, operational costs, and network emissions when integrated with an effective power management system, unlike EVs, which lack such a capability. Furthermore, RESs outperform DRPs in reducing these indices, as they are the primary injectors of both active and reactive power into FRIES or SDN. Consequently, under these conditions, the power and energy drawn from the upstream network decrease compared to case I, leading to reductions in energy losses, costs, and emissions. While DRPs merely shift peak energy consumption to off-peak or mid-peak hours. EVs increase overall energy demand from the upstream grid, which raises losses, costs, and emissions according to Fig. 7(a). Regarding voltage profile improvements based on Fig. 7(b), DRPs and EVs in case studies III and IV reduced the maximum voltage drop from 0.163 per unit in case 1 to 0.093 and 0.083 per unit, respectively, under the worst-case scenario (UL = 0.45) without causing overvoltage issues. In contrast, RESs have slightly induced a maximum overvoltage of 0.043 per unit in SDN to further reduce the voltage drop to 0.081 per unit at UL = 0.45. This is because RESs inject both active and reactive power into the system, while EVs only contribute reactive power and DRPs mainly redistribute energy during different load periods. Thus, in terms of voltage profile enhancement, RESs hold the highest priority, followed by EVs and then DRPs. In measuring harmonic index performance through TVH, case I reported a value of approximately 571.3 p.u. To mitigate TVH, significant contributions were observed from RESs (case II) and EVs (case IV), with RESs demonstrating superior harmonic control capabilities compared to EVs. DRPs did not impact harmonic management since they do not directly control harmonic currents; hence, TVH remained unchanged at 571.3 p.u. Concerning voltage stability through VSI, RESs showed superior ability to improve VSI compared to EVs, which in turn outperformed DRPs. This is attributed to the active and reactive power injection provided by RESs, whereas EVs supply only reactive power and DRPs deliver active power. Ultimately, the proposed system from case V, which integrates effective management of RES and other flexible resources (FRIES), demonstrated notable improvements across all performance indices under challenging conditions (UL = 0.45 and UB = 1). Specifically: Energy losses were reduced by approximately 45.4% ((60.16 – 32.83)/60.16) compared to case I, Maximum voltage drop decreased by around 57.7% under a maximum overvoltage of 0.018 per unit when compared to the initial scenario., TVH declined by roughly 48.6% relative to the load flow study in case I. Additionally, other metrics such as VSI, network emissions, and SDN operating costs improved by approximately 15%, 49.3%, and 55.2%, respectively.
Conclusion
This study introduces an optimized SDN power management approach within the framework of FRIES, addressing nonlinear load harmonic correction. The proposed system integrates renewable unit such as wind and photovoltaic systems, alongside flexible resources like demand response and electric vehicles aggregation. Employing a weighted sum of functions technique, a deterministic model was developed based on a four-objective optimization strategy. The objectives include minimizing total voltage harmonic, grid energy costs, and SDN emissions, while maximizing the voltage stability index. The model operates under constraints dictated by the behavior of RESs and flexible resources in FRIES, and linearized AC-HOPF equations. Uncertainties involving load variations, energy costs, RES outputs, and EV energy usage were incorporated using adaptive robust optimization. Results demonstrate that while non-linear solvers for this model exhibit varied solutions, linear solvers achieve a unique optimal solution with greater computational efficiency. Among the tested linear problem solvers, the CPLEX solver delivered the shortest computation time. The proposed architecture withstands a forecast error margin of up to 45%, accommodating uncertainties in demand, energy prices, RES power, and EV energy consumption while consistently reaching optimal outcomes. At the compromise point, key performance indicators show significant improvement: operating cost, network emissions, and total voltage harmonics are nearly minimized, while voltage stability approaches its maximum achievable value. Specifically, SDN operational costs, grid emissions, and voltage harmonics are approximately 14.8%, 43.5%, and 31.6% higher, or voltage stability index 32.1% lower relative to their ideal targets. When compared to load flow studies under the worst-case scenario with a 45% uncertainty level, the proposed design significantly mitigates grid energy losses, voltage drop, harmonic distortion, operational costs, and network emissions by roughly 45.4%, 57.7%, 48.6%, 55.2%, and 49.3%, respectively. Voltage stability also sees an improvement of approximately 15%, showcasing the effectiveness of active and reactive power management coupled with harmonic flow optimization in the FRIES framework.
